subject: Frontier-model routing, authorization drift, agent Postgres
preheader: Plus: 5 papers, an Anthropic harness postmortem, 2 X posts. 5 min.
title: Only 7% of agent turns needed a frontier model, and authorization drifts down hierarchies

story.title: How many of your agent's calls actually need a frontier model?
story.summary: LangChain benchmarks NVIDIA's NeMo Switchyard router on 145 agent tasks, measuring how often a turn required a frontier model and what routing the rest elsewhere saves.

lead.what: LangChain benchmarked NVIDIA's NeMo Switchyard, a model router, on 145 agent tasks. Only 7% of turns needed a frontier model.
lead.details: With the router escalating only when needed, routing cut cost 74% in exchange for six points of accuracy. The expensive model stops being the loop and becomes one worker inside it.
lead.yes_but: Six accuracy points isn't a rounding error, and this is one router on one 145-task suite. Whether your agent's turn mix looks like LangChain's is the question the benchmark can't answer.
lead.why: In LangChain's 145-task benchmark, only 7% of turns needed a frontier model. Routing cut cost 74%; whether the accuracy haircut is affordable depends on your workload.

items.title: MasDrift: Benchmarking Authorization Preservation Across Multi-Agent Architectures
items.summary: MasDrift runs 600 benign productivity tasks with reserved actions through single agents, hierarchies, and peer networks. Hierarchies completed more tasks but took unauthorized actions in 2.7–19.8% of tasks versus 0.6–0.8% for peer networks, a gap that widens with depth.

items.title: An AI Scientist that Doesn't Drift: Taste, Structure, and Falsifiable Findings in a Quadruped Navigation Research Loop
items.summary: A research loop built against drift: immutable experiment cards so a falsified hypothesis can't be retconned, subagents locked to mechanical roles, and a preference oracle that alone makes subjective calls. The oracle changed research direction, not the best score.

items.title: AndroidReality: How Far Are Mobile Agents from the Real World?
items.summary: AndroidReality injects realistic state, transition, and action perturbations into AndroidWorld to measure how far mobile agents fall from their clean-benchmark numbers. It finds substantial failure gaps and a training-free recovery step that helps in both settings.

items.title: Controlled Memory Interference in Continual LLM Agents
items.summary: A diagnostic framework for when an agent's new information fails to overwrite the old. Relationship-specific interference sharply suppresses memory updates with little stability gain, and lexical and dense retrieval fail through distinct pathways.

items.title: When LLM Agents Negotiate: Private Information and Dynamic Bargaining in Supply Chains
items.summary: Nine LLMs negotiated 9,840 buyer-seller contracts against a game-theoretic benchmark. Agents captured 95.4% of first-best surplus, but slow bargaining eroded 21–34% of it, and baseline models accepted individually irrational contracts in 19.2% of cases.

items.title: TDD inside the agent loop - theater or actual value?
items.summary: Birgitta Böckeler at Thoughtworks ran experiments on whether telling a coding agent to use TDD changes the outcome or only imitates a favored process.

items.title: Evolution of agentic surfaces
items.summary: Anthropic's Applied AI team on harness assumptions going stale: a context-reset workaround built for Sonnet 4.5 became pure overhead once Opus 4.5 shipped without the quirk. Decoupling the agent loop from tool execution cut time to first token 60% at P50 and over 90% at P95.

items.title: Databricks Acquires Electric to Give Every AI Agent its Own Postgres
items.summary: Databricks is acquiring ElectricSQL to embed a full Postgres inside every AI-agent sandbox, syncing local state back to its Lakebase platform.
